title: Chapter 22: Everyone Who Ever Crossed
content: The county copier jams on page sixty-three.

Wren has counted the jams now. Sixty-three, one hundred and four, two hundred and eleven. The machine does not like the middle of the book, which is where the water got in, and every sheet it gives her has a grey shadow down one edge like a bruise.
"Again," Mars says.
"Again."

It is twenty past four on a Monday morning, and the records room in the courthouse basement is the warmest place in Kestrel Bend, which is not a compliment. The radiator ticks. The far tube in the ceiling light has gone pink at one end. Upstairs a janitor is working the second floor, and he has been told that the clerk is staying late, and at his age he has decided not to ask.

Mars plugs the telephone into the machine with a cable she has carried in her bag since September, because county copiers do not talk to telephones, and Mars has never accepted that a thing cannot be made to.
"Ten pages to a sheet," she says. "Four columns. Names at seven point."
"Six for the dates."
"Nobody reads six point."
"Nobody has to read it at home. They have to read it standing up at a window with nothing else to do."

That is the design. Forty sheets. Four hundred and two pages of the crossing log, every name from the twelfth of April 1908 to the twelfth of September 2026, printed small enough that a person has to come close to the glass.

She has thought about the order for three nights. Alphabetical would be tidier and would hide everything, because a town read alphabetically is a town that has never lost anybody. So the sheets go in time. 1908 first, nine names in brown ink. Then the war years, when the ferry ran with a lamp because the young men were gone. Then 1961, when the log has three pages for one day and the water column says plus eleven. Then the long flat middle of the century, names she has never heard and names she hears every morning at the diner.

The fares go on too. She has decided to leave nothing out. Not the margins. Not the nineteen afternoons with no siren written in pencil. Not the four hundred and eleven IOUs, the word repeated down the columns in her grandfather's small left-leaning hand, as if the town's debt were a kind of weather.

At half past five the machine eats page two hundred and eleven, and Mars takes the side panel off with a screwdriver from her bag and puts her hand inside, up to the wrist, and pulls out a page folded like an accordion.
"County paper," she says. "County toner. County machine."
"On a service contract the county pays for."
"Which nobody will ask about."
"Which nobody will ask about."
Mars feeds it again. The page comes out clean. She sets it on the pile and looks at it, and then at Wren.
"You know what this is," she says. "This is not a protest. A protest is a sign. This is a document."
"It is a copy."
"It is a copy of an original the county has refused to certify." Mars squares the corner. "In this building that is the same as a shot across the bow."
"Mars."
"I am not going to cry about my job before I lose it."
"I was going to say thank you."

"Then say it at eight, when I am at my desk and I can be seen being normal." She feeds another page. "If they ask me where the toner went, I am going to say I do not know what toner is. I have been practicing."

They carry the box up the back stairs at twenty to seven, Mars in her hood with her shoulders up like a person doing something, which she is. The morning is the first one with real winter in it. The puddles by the loading bay have a skin on them. Wren's hands are red before they reach the street.
Mars holds the box on the step while Wren starts on the Annex, nine sheets across the queue window, four across the door, one on the glass beside the bell.

The tape will not stick to cold glass. She has to lay her palm flat on each pane and count to twenty, warming it, before the strip will hold. By the third window she cannot feel her fingers. By the fifth she is using the heel of her hand.
At four minutes to seven Hollis Drane comes up Third Street with his coat buttoned wrong and his keys already out.
He stops. He is a small man in a good coat, and he stands there with his mouth open like a person doing arithmetic he does not like the answer to.
"Miss Aubrey."
"Mr. Drane."
"This is a public building."
"It is." She presses the last strip flat. "The public is outside it."
He looks at the nearest sheet. He looks a long time. Then his hand comes up without him telling it to, and his finger finds a line in the middle of 1988.
"June the ninth," he says. "Six forty in the morning."
"Yes."
"He spelled my name wrong." The finger stays where it is. "Drane with an e. He has me as Drain. Thirty-eight years and I never told him."
"Would you like a pen?"
Hollis looks at her then, and his face does something complicated and is put away, the way it always is.
"No," he says. "I would like to open my office."

He goes in. He does not take anything down. Through the glass she watches him hang his coat on the hook and sit at the second desk with his back to the window, and the queue forms behind him at eight, and every person in it reads over his shoulder.
By nine the diner is full of people standing up.
Ruthie Pyle comes out with her ledger under her arm and stands in front of the six sheets taped across the two front windows, and reads them with her glasses on the end of her nose.

"Nineteen fifty-three," she says. "Pell. That is Otis's father. He went in at the landing in a squall and they told Otis the boat turned." She turns a page of her own book, finds nothing, and puts the pen back in her apron. "I have that in here as the boat turning."
"It may have turned."

"It may have." Ruthie looks at the sheet again. "But there is a difference between a boat turning and a river standing up inside it, and this town has been paying for the wrong one since before I was born."
She does not write anything down. It is the first time Wren has ever seen her not write anything down, and it frightens her more than the Authority does.
At ten Otis Pell comes.

He is eighty-four and walks with two sticks and does not say a word to anybody. He stands in front of the 1953 column with one finger on the paper, the way a man holds a door for somebody behind him, and stays there for eleven minutes.
Then he says, "That is my father," to nobody in particular, and a woman in the queue says, "We know, Otis," and he says, "No. That is my father's name, written down," and the queue stops talking.
By half past ten there is coffee.

Nobody organizes it. A man in a feed cap puts a cardboard tray of cups on the low wall by the steps and does not say who it is for. A woman comes out of the bank with a plate of sandwiches and sets it down and goes back in. The queue eats standing up and reads the windows and somebody laughs at a fare of five cents and then stops laughing.
At eleven a woman in a quilted coat comes up to Wren with a plastic bag.
"Are you the one doing this?"
"Yes."
"Hold out your hand."
In the bag is a stamp. Wooden handle, black body, the kind you order from a catalogue, with a rubber die cut to read CERTIFIED in a serif nobody chose.
"I bought it in August for a different reason," the woman says. "That reason did not work out. Nothing in this town is real until it is stamped, so now you have a stamp."
Wren turns it over. It is heavier than it looks, and the rubber smells new, and the word sits upside down in the little window at the top.
"Thank you."
"Put it on the paper. Not on your hand."

She takes the cap off and stamps the top corner of the last sheet, 2026, page four hundred and two, and the word comes out clean and black and a little crooked, and the woman, who turns out to be named Junie Hale and has lived four streets over for thirty years, says, "There," and walks off down Third Street.
At noon the Authority truck parks across the street.
Two men get out. One is young and carries a plastic barrel. The older one has a putty knife and a scraper and the patient face of a man who has removed other people's paper before.
"Ma'am," he says. "I am sorry about this."
"You are not."
"No," he agrees. "But it is the sentence they give us."

He works from the left. The sheets come away in long curls, and the tape takes some of the paint with it, and he stacks them flat in the barrel in the order he takes them, which Wren appreciates, because it means he has thought about it.
"Keep them dry," she says. "It is going to rain at four."
He looks at the sky.
"It is."
"Then keep them dry."

He puts the lid on the barrel. The young one does the diner and the landing and the boat shed and the church board, and it takes an hour and ten minutes, and the whole street watches, and nobody says anything to them, and the older man says "ma'am" again when he is finished, and they drive off with forty sheets of the town's dead in a barrel in the bed of a truck.
At four it rains.
At six it stops. Wren walks down to the landing with a torch and finds the piling bare and the boat shed sheet gone and the water up half a foot and brown.
Then she walks back up Mill Street and stops in the middle of the road.

There are sheets in the diner windows. Sheets on the church door. Sheets on the school fence and the glass of the gas station and the board outside the post office. And there are sheets on the wall of the Annex again, taped high, above the reach of a putty knife, in strips of the good tape.
The copies are copies of copies. The names have gone soft at the edges. Somebody has run them on the school machine and somebody else has cut them down to fit.
Wren counts them, because counting is what she does.
Forty-one.
The forty-first is on the boat shed, at eye height, dry under the eave.
It is blank except for one line at the top, in pencil, in a hand she knows from the back of a grocery list on her own kitchen table.
Ade Kessler. 22 Oct 2026.
Under the name there is nothing, because there is no record to print. The rest of the sheet is empty, and the empty part is the whole point.
highlight: Forty sheets of the crossing log go up across town, and by evening there are forty-one.
